doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: Stopping time with Scott and listening in improvised ensemble
summary: Orin's time limit, Scott pushing to stop, and listening and responding in group improvisation.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah Orin said, he told me we could go to 11, and then Scott heard, somebody told Scott that we had to stop at 10:30. So Scott was trying to stop us at 10:30 and then his wife said well why don’t we just go to quarter to 11. She split the difference. So I was working towards, well I figured I didn’t want to go to quarter to 11, I wanted to go to ten to 11, but Scott wanted to stop at 10:30. And I kept hearing for him pushing. Well that’s what I’m saying. I mean each musician can push us to stop. And they push us to go. They can push us to go out, they can push us to go in. They can push us to be sensitive, they can push us to be hard, they can push us to be harsh you know, depending on what they do. Because we feed off each other. We feed off each other. So if I hear Warren really pushing then I know I’ve got to push you know. If I hear him backing off then I know I can back off and everything. Same thing with Scott. So that’s the interaction of music just like we’re interacting right now. You know if I say something funny, you know you’ll have to make a determination whether you’re going to laugh or not, right. But it’s the same type of thing, you know, because if I say something to insult you then all of a sudden it’s a whole different reaction. So it’s the same type of thing here. That’s the thing about the power of improvised music is that it builds the brain in a different sort of way. Because at the same time, because you have the skill, I can see it, you have the skill to listen and speak at the same time. A lot of people don’t have that you know. Once they start talking their ears shut down. And that’s the whole thing about playing music. As you’re playing you have to listen to what’s going on around you because if you don’t then why are you playing and who are you playing with? And I know, I blame some bands and musicians, when they tell me that when they sing their part they don’t hear, or they play it, they don’t hear it. I say how could you exist on the stage like that, where you don’t hear what’s going on with the rest of the band. All you just concentrate on what you are doing. I said how could you exist like that. I mean but you end up finding out that those musicians are very, very rigid. Because the band begins to bend and begins to do different things and these people don’t, they just like — my part — they’re just driving their part along even though the band might slow down or whatever, they don’t slow down. They just drive their thing. And it’s harsh. It’s very very harsh. It’s a very very harsh reality. But some people don’t have that skill where they can listen and talk at the same time, or they can play and listen to what the other musicians are playing and assimilate a change when that person changes and then you make a change at the same time, not based on visual cues or anything, just based on a person hearing that okay this person made a change, he’s going faster, he’s going slower, he’s playing louder, he’s playing softer. And then you make that change

and everything. And that’s what I love about this ensemble. We have the ability to do that type of thing where we can change on a dime based on input from any one of us. And then if we expand the ensemble and get other musicians of the same type of sensitivity, they will have the same inputs.
